question: Practitioners of this practice are sometimes divided into non-spiritual users, who slip potions into a target's food or drink, and spiritual ones, who work through a Taoist sorcerer capable of summoning ghosts or demons. It is believed to fuse poison-based techniques said to originate in Yunnan, China with indigenous spirit sorcery from maritime Southeast Asia, and is typically sought out by those chasing revenge, mending a relationship, or solving money troubles. A Singaporean who suddenly falls ill or starts acting strangely might be described as having been 'tio' this, meaning they were struck by it. In Hokkien, Teochew and Cantonese, this term names the folk practice blamed for unexplained misfortune, illness or bad luck. For 10 points, give this Singlish and Southeast Asian term for black magic or witchcraft used to curse a victim.

At these Singaporean nightlife venues, patrons traditionally buy a floral garland to present to a hostess, paying for her company and conversation over drinks rather than for admission alone. Its name combines the historic name for Thailand with a Cantonese word meaning 'to hang,' a reference to how the garland is worn around the hostess's neck. Smaller and cozier than a typical discotheque, these lounges favor slow, mellow Chinese pop known as manyao over club anthems. For 10 points, give this two-word Singlish term for a Thai-themed hostess lounge, named for the Southeast Asian country formerly known by a different name.

Literally invoking a garden tool, this Cantonese curse wishes its target's whole family scooped up and buried, using a verb that normally means 'to shovel.' Its first two syllables, on their own, simply mean 'whole family,' while the profanity comes from the final word. Roughly as harsh in tone as calling someone 'a piece of shit,' it ranks among the most common vulgarities in Cantonese, heard in Singapore, Hong Kong and wherever the dialect is spoken. For 10 points, give this three-syllable Cantonese curse, roughly translated as 'may your whole family be shoveled into a grave.'
answer: ham ga chan [or ham gaa caan; or hum ka chan]

question: A dessert cafe at a CapitaLand mall has an English name that translates this Hokkien phrase. In 2023, Singaporean rapper ShiGGa Shay released a drill track bearing this title alongside Taiwanese rapper E.SO. Rooted in racing jargon, its literal meaning describes a race with no rival left to challenge the winner. Singaporeans tack it onto the end of a compliment, saying someone is 'zai until' this phrase, to mean they are impossibly good. For 10 points, give this Hokkien idiom, used to call something unrivaled or without equal.
answer: bo beh zao [or boh beh zao; or bo beh zau; or no horse run]

question: This nightclub's eight-cabin Ferris wheel, nicknamed 'The Big Q,' looks down on the dance floor, while guests can also ride a slide called 'Sunny Slide Up' down from its third floor. Its brand was founded in New York in 2003 before opening locations in Las Vegas and Sydney, and its local branch, opened in July 2019 by TAO Group Hospitality, marked the brand's first expansion into Asia. Built inside space once occupied by one of Marina Bay Sands' Broadway-style theatres, its roughly 2,300-square-metre floor and 30-metre ceilings make it the city-state's largest nightclub. For 10 points, name this nightclub at Marina Bay Sands, known for its Ferris wheel and giant slide.

Twenty shophouses along Syed Alwi Road were demolished to make way for this business's flagship building, a 45-million-dollar, 75,000-square-foot department store completed in 1995 that also included a 130-room hotel. It began in 1971 as a Campbell Lane retail store selling ready-made clothing, founded by Mustaq Ahmad together with his father and uncle Samsuddin. Since 2003 it has stayed open 24 hours a day, drawing shoppers to its Little India location for everything from groceries and electronics to garments and gold. For 10 points, name this sprawling round-the-clock shopping complex in Little India, Singapore.

Tables spill into the back alley behind this eatery's original shophouse on Jalan Besar, which has since expanded to occupy four connecting shophouse units at that address. Long known for staying open into the small hours, it now closes at 2am on weeknights and 4am on weekends, though it is shut every Tuesday. Established in 1962, it has grown from that single Jalan Besar location to outlets in Tampines, Changi Airport, and beyond. For 10 points, name this Singapore eatery, a favorite among students and night owls for its late-night small plates.

This cinema's original building opened in February 1959 in a grand ceremony attended by the Prime Minister of Malaya and Britain's Commissioner for Southeast Asia, and was billed as the most luxurious cinema in Singapore. That original venue and the office tower beside it were torn down around 1990 to make way for a new complex bearing the same names, which reopened in May 1993 with five cinemas. Expansions in 1996 brought it to eight halls, and the studio behind both buildings has operated it on Orchard Road since 1958. For 10 points, name this cinema inside an Orchard Road shopping complex, a longtime Orchard Road landmark.
answer: Shaw Theatres Lido [or Lido Theatre; or Shaw Lido; or Lido]

question: Until 1999, Singapore's Ministry of Education called this programme by a name suggesting it was optional add-on learning; the rename that year was meant to signal it as integral to education instead. Every secondary school student must take part in one, choosing from four groupings: clubs and societies, physical sports, uniformed groups, and visual and performing arts. It is compulsory at the secondary level and encouraged, but not required, in primary and post-secondary schools. For 10 points, give this abbreviation for the after-school clubs, sports, and uniformed groups Singapore students take part in outside the classroom.

Borrowed from a Cantonese verb meaning 'to pack,' this Singlish term shares roots with a Malaysian slang variant, though some trace its Singapore usage instead to Hokkien. Central to hawker centre culture, it describes asking a stallholder to pack your order into a container or bag instead of eating in. A Singaporean running late might tell a friend to just do this to the food and bring it home rather than dine in. For 10 points, give this Singlish verb, with several spellings, meaning to get food to take away.

This Singlish verb's Hokkien root, fang sheng, literally names the Buddhist practice of releasing captive animals back into the wild for merit. Singaporeans stretched its meaning to cover backing out of a commitment at the last minute, leaving the other party in the lurch. A friend who agrees to meet up and then cancels without warning might be accused of doing this. For 10 points, give this Singlish verb for standing someone up or bailing on an arrangement.

Borrowed from a Malay word meaning 'above,' this Singlish adjective describes something or someone perceived as high-class, fancy or upmarket. Depending on tone, it can be a compliment for a swanky restaurant or a dig at someone acting snobbish and looking down on others. A condominium with a rooftop infinity pool, or a hipster cafe charging eight dollars for kopi, might equally be called this. For 10 points, give this Singlish adjective for something posh, high-class or above the average Singaporean's usual haunts.

Singaporean national servicemen might hear an instructor bark this phrase at recruits who stand around watching their platoon mates struggle with a task instead of pitching in. Wives use it just as sarcastically on husbands who watch television instead of helping with the housework. The phrase implies that merely looking at a task, rather than lending a hand, could somehow get it done through sheer optical force. For 10 points, give this two-word Singlish phrase for idly watching instead of helping, as if your eyes alone could do the work.

In 2013, a video of an unnamed auntie describing a passing storm went viral, earning her the nickname 'Grape Auntie' for likening the falling drops to grapes before escalating to this exclamation. The clip was later turned into a dance remix titled after this quote by the local group Fallen Superhero SG. Describing an unusually intense downpour, it observes that the size of the raindrops has apparently reached that of a frozen kitchen staple. For 10 points, give this viral 2013 Singlish quote in which an auntie marvels that the downpour has produced chunks of frozen water.

In a 2016 episode of Crimewatch, an underworld leader called Ah Xiong rejects a recruit's given name as insufficiently intimidating, drawing out its pronunciation until it sounds almost like 'Meowvin.' He renames the recruit 'Xiao Hu,' or 'Little Tiger,' instead. Clipped and recirculated years later, the scene became one of the docu-drama's most memed moments, spawning parodies with the rejected name swapped for others. For 10 points, give this quote, spoken by a fictional Crimewatch boss, dismissing a common English first name as unsuitable for a hardened criminal.
answer: Melvin is no name for a gangster [or Melvin is no name for a gang member]

question: This line was delivered by actress Jernelle Oh to co-star Shanice Koh during a confrontation between two rival gang members in a May 2013 episode of Crimewatch titled 'Gang Clash.' Its over-the-top delivery and soap-opera intensity turned the scene into an internet sensation when clips resurfaced on TikTok in 2021, prompting both actresses to reenact it themselves years later. For 10 points, give this line hurled as an insult in a viral Crimewatch clip, accusing a fellow character of a particular profession.

Its literal sense names a traditional shadow-puppet theatre performance found across Java and the wider Malay world. Singaporeans repurposed the word to describe putting on an insincere show, such as suddenly looking busy the moment a supervisor walks by. It resurfaces every election season, when candidates accused of empty gestures for the cameras are said to be doing this. For 10 points, give this Singlish word, borrowed from Malay and ultimately Javanese, for a performative, insincere show put on to impress or deceive.

Announced at the 2018 National Day Rally, an 8-billion-dollar scheme for the younger of these two paired groups launched the following year, while its older counterpart's own 9-billion-dollar scheme had already launched in 2014. Together, the two schemes give qualifying seniors MediSave top-ups, subsidised outpatient care and other benefits in recognition of their contributions during Singapore's early nation-building years. Membership in the older group is generally defined by citizenship obtained before independence, while the younger group covers citizens born in the 1950s who later became citizens. For 10 points, name either of this pair of Singaporean government support schemes for senior citizens, one honouring early nation-builders and the other named with the Malay word for 'independence.'
answer: Pioneer Generation [or Merdeka Generation; or Pioneer Generation Package; or Merdeka Generation Package]

question: On 16 December 2020, UNESCO inscribed the tradition surrounding these community dining spaces onto its intangible heritage list, Singapore's first entry on that list. Bringing food from Chinese, Malay, Indian and other culinary traditions together under one roof, they were described by UNESCO as 'community dining rooms' that reflect Singapore's diverse, urban character. Found in almost every Singaporean neighbourhood, they replaced the itinerant street food vendors of the mid-20th century with fixed, licensed stalls. For 10 points, name these open-air complexes of food stalls, an iconic fixture of everyday life across Singapore.
answer: hawker centre [or hawker centres; or hawker culture; or hawker center]

question: This stall's chicken rice was praised by chef Anthony Bourdain as so fragrant it could be eaten on its own, without any accompaniment. It has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand every year since 2016 and famously beat Gordon Ramsay in a televised cook-off in 2013. Operating out of the Maxwell Food Centre since 1986, its name means 'day after day,' or roughly 'every day,' in Mandarin. For 10 points, name this famous Hainanese chicken rice stall, a fixture of Maxwell Food Centre often mobbed by long queues.
answer: Tian Tian Chicken Rice [or Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice]

question: During a January 2024 US congressional hearing on TikTok and child online safety, Tom Cotton repeatedly pressed the platform's chief executive about his nationality and any ties to the Chinese Communist Party. The executive, born and raised in the city-state before working in Silicon Valley and London, grew visibly exasperated as he repeated this flat correction. CNN's clip of the exchange, posted that February, went viral and gave locals a rallying cry whenever their nationality was questioned or conflated with a neighboring country. For 10 points, give this quote in which TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew corrects a US lawmaker questioning his nationality.

This narration accompanies a dramatized gold-necklace-snatching scene from a 1998 episode of Crimewatch, describing the victim's reaction to the theft in flat, deadpan English. A TikTok user reposted the clip in June 2021, and by that October a second, even more popular repost had turned the line into a go-to audio meme for expressing disbelief or shock. For 10 points, give this narrator's line from a decades-old Crimewatch scene, describing a robbery victim's reaction, now used across TikTok whenever Singaporeans want to convey speechless shock.
answer: The Woman Was Too Stunned to Speak [or Too Stunned to Speak]

question: Produced jointly by the National Crime Prevention Council and the Singapore Police Force, this programme presents dramatised re-enactments of real criminal cases alongside appeals for help solving unsolved ones. It airs in four separate language editions on Mediacorp's Channel 5, Channel 8, Suria and Vasantham, each with its own presenting team of real, serving police officers. First broadcast on 30 November 1986, it is Singapore's longest-running info-educational television programme, having reached its 40th season by 2026. Several of its dramatised scenes, including arguments between rival gang members, have gone on to become internet memes decades after first airing. For 10 points, name this long-running Singaporean crime-prevention docu-drama series.

This road's name literally means "pineapple" in Hokkien, itself a pun on a homophonous phrase meaning "fortune arrives," which made the fruit especially auspicious in traditional Chinese culture. It lies in Serangoon, near a neighboring road named after another once-locally-grown fruit, durian, called by its own Hokkien name. A park bearing the same name as this lane now sits nearby. For 10 points, name this quirky Serangoon road name, whose literal Hokkien meaning is a fruit associated with good fortune.

This politician served in the Singapore Armed Forces from 1987 to 2011, rising to Chief of Army before entering politics. After winning a seat in Tanjong Pagar GRC in the 2011 general election, he became Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress from 2015 to 2018. He then served as Minister for Trade and Industry from 2018 to 2021 and Minister for Education from 2021 to 2025, before being appointed Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence in May 2025. A President's Scholar, he graduated with First Class Honours in Economics from Christ's College, Cambridge. For 10 points, name this Singaporean Cabinet minister and former Chief of Army.

the island's colonial founder convened a meeting on 1 April 1823 to propose founding this school, then laying its foundation stone that June with the stated aim of educating the children of local leaders and collecting the "scattered literature and traditions of the country." It has since produced 96 President's Scholars along with three of the country's presidents and five of its prime ministers. Alumni beyond the political sphere include lawyer and social reformer Song Ong Siang and diplomat Tommy Koh. For 10 points, name this school founded by the island's colonial founder, originally named for its host city.

This politician earned a Bachelor's degree in Mathematics and a Diploma in Computer Science from Cambridge before becoming a Mason Fellow at Harvard's Kennedy School. Before entering politics, he served in the Singapore Armed Forces, retiring as a Brigadier-General. First elected to Parliament in 1984, he chaired the Monetary Authority of Singapore from 1998 to 2004 while also serving as Deputy Prime Minister. His first wife, Wong Ming Yang, died in 1982; he remarried Ho Ching in 1985. For 10 points, name this politician who served as Singapore's third Prime Minister from 2004 to 2024, son of the country's founding Prime Minister.

According to the Sejarah Melayu, or Malay Annals, this 13th-century Palembang prince of the Srivijaya royal house spotted a strange red-bodied, black-headed, white-breasted animal that vanished into the jungle upon landing on the island of Temasek around 1299. His chief minister, Demang Lebar Daun, identified the creature as a lion, and taking this as a good omen, the prince founded a city there and renamed the island using the Sanskrit words for "Lion City." Since actual lions have never lived in the region, historians generally believe the animal he really saw was a Malayan tiger. For 10 points, name this legendary founder of Singapura, who according to legend named the island "Lion City" after his lion sighting.

This three-word Hokkien exclamation combines words meaning "lucky," "prosperous," and "to flourish." It is traditionally shouted while diners use their chopsticks to toss a raw fish salad as high as possible above the table, a Chinese New Year custom called lo hei that Singapore's Cantonese community originally practiced privately on the seventh day of the new year before restaurants commercialized it with elaborate set menus. Participants believe that shouting louder and tossing higher will bring greater prosperity in the coming year. For 10 points, give this auspicious Hokkien phrase, wishing for luck, prosperity and success, shouted during the yusheng-tossing ritual.

This dish's glutinous, starchy gravy gets its body from a stream of beaten egg poured in near the end of cooking, after the braising liquid has been thickened with tapioca or corn starch and spiced with five-spice powder, cinnamon, and star anise. Brought to Singapore by Fujianese immigrants, it is traditionally topped with fish cake, braised pork, and a hard-boiled egg, then finished with a squeeze of kalamansi, minced garlic, and red vinegar for tang. Hawker stalls across the island serve bowls of it alongside crispy ngo hiang or fried fritters. For 10 points, name this thick, starchy Hokkien noodle dish whose name literally means "braised noodles."

This Singlish adjective derives from a Malay word originally meaning "torn" or "ragged." Singaporeans use it to describe anything chaotic, messy, or disastrously out of control, whether it's a hectic work week, a wild party, or unbearably hot weather. Millennials often clip it to "rabs" or "rabz" in text messages, a shortened form that spawned a newer rhyming Gen-Z phrase pairing it with a Middle Eastern food item. For 10 points, name this Singlish slang term for something wild, messy, or out of hand.

This rhyming Singlish phrase emerged as a playful extension of a shorter, decades-old slang word ending in "-ak," clipped down to a near-homophone of its first syllable before a rhyming word was tacked on. An AsiaOne feature on the "creative evolution" of Singlish cited it as an example of how younger Singaporeans remix existing slang into new reduplicative forms. Despite its second word, it has no connection to Turkish or Middle Eastern food. For 10 points, name this Gen-Z Singlish expression, a rhyming spin-off of "rabak" that also means chaotic or out of control.

These transient bazaars, whose Malay name refers to their after-dark hours, trace back to weekly gatherings organized by itinerant hawkers in 1950s Singapore, though the term only gained widespread use from the 1960s. Once a common sight in housing estates after dark, they were phased out in 1978 amid concerns over traffic jams, pollution, and hygiene, which pushed street hawkers into purpose-built hawker centres instead. Despite this, they have made periodic comebacks at void decks, carparks, and open fields across the island. For 10 points, name this Malay term for a roving after-dark bazaar selling street food, toys, and cheap wares.

This constituency was Singapore's longest continuously opposition-held ward, represented by a single MP from 1984 to 2011. Chiam See Tong, first of the Singapore Democratic Party and later the Singapore Democratic Alliance, held this seat for 27 years, serving for much of that time as the de facto Leader of the Opposition. In 2011, the PAP's Sitoh Yih Pin narrowly defeated Chiam's wife Lina here by just 114 votes, ending the ward's decades of opposition control. For 10 points, name this Singapore constituency whose name literally means "cut sand" in Malay.

This pre-university school's foundation stone was laid by Tan Sri Runme Shaw in December 1976 at Malan Road, following a joint building effort by the Anglican, Lutheran, and Presbyterian churches. It traces its roots to a secondary school founded by the Anglican Diocese of Singapore in 1862, and its first six hundred students were admitted to the Arts and Science faculties in January 1978 under founding principal Reverend John Tan Teng Wai. It was officially declared open by Tan Sri Runme Shaw in June 1979. For 10 points, give the abbreviation for this Anglican pre-university school.
answer: SAJC [or St Andrew's Junior College; or Saint Andrew's Junior College]

question: This green space traces its origins to an 1822 experimental horticultural project Stamford Raffles set up at Fort Canning, before the present site was laid out in the English Landscape style by an Agri-Horticultural Society in 1859 and later handed to the colonial government in 1874. In July 2015, it became the first tropical site of its kind and third such site in the world to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This 82-hectare park along Cluny Road is home to a nationally known orchid display. For 10 points, name this park in the city-state, the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.
